implementation_notes: The document is a plain Go struct and encoding/json is the codec: json.Marshal writes it with wire names fixed by json:"field,omitempty" tags, and json.Unmarshal fills a fresh struct and returns an error instead of throwing, so a malformed document is an ordinary error path. Use json.NewDecoder with UseNumber when large integers must not be rounded into float64, and keep wire DTOs separate from domain structs because the exported-field rule decides what is serialized. This is the default Go realization: no code generation, no dependency, and the struct itself is the document contract.
pitfalls: Unmarshal maps every JSON number to float64 by default, so large identifiers lose precision; decode into string-typed ids or with a Decoder using UseNumber.
A typo in a struct tag is not a compile error: the field silently marshals under its Go name, and unknown incoming fields are dropped without warning.
Unexported fields are skipped and nil slices or pointers do not round-trip as expected (omitted versus null), so optional-field semantics must be chosen deliberately.
Reusing domain structs as wire documents couples the contract to internal refactors and lets stray fields leak to consumers.

variants.name: protoc-gen-go generated message types
variants.implementation_notes: When the document contract is shared across languages, the schema lives in a .proto file and protoc-gen-go generates Go types (Open struct API or the recommended opaque API) together with the protobuf wire encoding; protojson marshals and unmarshals the same messages as proto3 JSON, which the standard encoding/json package does not implement. Choose this route when field-number evolution and cross-language contracts matter more than the zero-dependency stdlib path; the cost is a protoc toolchain in the build plus generated code in the repository.
pitfalls: The generated .pb.go files and the protobuf runtime version are coupled: regenerate in CI or the build breaks after a runtime upgrade.
protojson output is proto3 JSON, not encoding/json output (field names, int64 as strings, well-known types), so swapping the two codecs changes the wire bytes.
Protobuf fields are presence-tracked with defaults; treating a zero value as absent silently loses explicit zeroes on both sides.
